items.q: The volcano (A) has erupted twice last century, (B) which is why the villages (C) on its slopes were (D) abandoned for decades.
items.explanation: Last century is a finished time, so the verb must be past simple (erupted); the present perfect cannot be used with a finished past time.

items.q: Our chemistry teacher insisted (A) that we wear goggles (B) during we were mixing the acids, (C) even though the experiment (D) took only a few minutes.
items.explanation: During is a preposition and needs a noun after it; a clause with a subject and verb needs the conjunction while.

items.q: The marathon runners (A) were exhausted after the race, (B) but they still spoke (C) proud about finishing (D) in such heavy rain.
items.explanation: The word describes how they spoke, so an adverb is needed: proudly, not the adjective proud.

items.q: Although the hotel (A) was cheap, the rooms (B) were clean and the staff (C) gave us (D) a few useful advices about the island.
items.explanation: Advice is an uncountable noun: it has no plural form and cannot follow a few; use some advice or a piece of advice.

items.q: (A) Each of the paintings in the gallery were painted by a student (B) who had never (C) studied art (D) before joining the club.
options: Each of the paintings in the gallery were painted
items.correction: Each of the paintings in the gallery was painted
items.explanation: The subject is each, which is singular, so the verb must be was; the plural noun after of does not change the agreement.

items.q: My cousin and (A) I have decided to (B) teach ourself how to cook (C) Thai food (D) by watching videos online.
items.explanation: The subject is plural (my cousin and I), so the reflexive pronoun must be the plural form ourselves; ourself is not a standard form.

items.q: The new stadium is (A) much bigger than the old one, (B) but many fans say (C) the atmosphere is not as lively than (D) it used to be.
options: the atmosphere is not as lively than
items.correction: the atmosphere is not as lively as
items.explanation: The equal comparison uses as ... as; than only follows a comparative form such as livelier.

items.q: The school (A) will hold the football final (B) on the main pitch tomorrow (C) as planned (D) unless it will rain heavily overnight.
items.explanation: After unless, if and other condition words we use the present simple for the future, never will: unless it rains.

items.q: The librarian (A) asked me that I had returned the dictionary (B) which I had borrowed (C) two weeks earlier, (D) but I had completely forgotten.
options: asked me that I had returned
items.correction: asked me whether I had returned
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question is introduced by whether or if, not that; that is used for reported statements.

items.q: My neighbour, (A) an elderly man (B) who his son is a famous chef in Hanoi, (C) still grows all his own vegetables (D) in a tiny garden.
options: who his son is a famous chef in Hanoi
still grows all his own vegetables
items.correction: whose son is a famous chef in Hanoi
items.explanation: To show possession in a relative clause we use whose; who his is never correct.

items.q: Nobody in our class (A) could understand (B) why (C) was the experiment so difficult (D) until the teacher explained it again.
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb: why the experiment was, not the inverted order of a direct question.

items.q: After the storm, volunteers (A) spent the whole weekend (B) clearing the beach (C) so that tourists could (D) make photos of the sunrise again.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is take a photo; make is not used with photo in English.

items.q: (A) The Mount Everest is so high (B) that climbers need extra oxygen (C) once they pass (D) a certain altitude.
items.explanation: Names of single mountains (Mount Everest, Mount Fuji) take no article; the is used only with mountain ranges such as the Alps.

items.q: (A) The museum stayed open late (B) despite it was raining heavily, (C) so we managed to see (D) every exhibition before closing time.
items.explanation: Despite is followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause needs the conjunction although (or despite the fact that).

items.q: By the time (A) the fire engine arrived, (B) the neighbours (C) already put out the flames (D) with buckets of water.
items.explanation: By the time + past simple signals an action completed earlier, so the main clause needs the past perfect: had already put out.

items.q: My sister has been (A) interested in astronomy (B) since she was ten, (C) and now she is (D) good in solving physics problems.
items.explanation: The adjective good takes the preposition at when it describes ability: good at something.

items.q: (A) Neither the coach nor the players was happy (B) with the referee's decision, (C) which cost the team (D) its place in the final.
options: Neither the coach nor the players was happy
items.correction: Neither the coach nor the players were happy
items.explanation: With neither ... nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; the players is plural, so the verb must be were.

items.q: Scientists warn that (A) plastic waste (B) is a serious threaten to sea turtles, (C) which often mistake bags (D) for jellyfish.
items.explanation: After a serious a noun is required: threat; threaten is the verb form.

items.q: The twins look (A) so alike that (B) even their teachers (C) sometimes cannot tell they apart (D) during the first weeks of term.
options: during the first weeks of term
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of tell ... apart, so the object form them is needed, not the subject form they.

items.q: This year's winter (A) has been (B) far colder than last year's, (C) and the mountain villages (D) received the most snow than ever before.
options: received the most snow than ever before
items.correction: received more snow than ever before
items.explanation: Than must follow a comparative (more snow); a superlative like the most is never combined with than.

items.q: (A) There were too much people at the concert, (B) so the organisers (C) had to close the gates (D) an hour early.
items.explanation: People is a plural countable noun, so the quantifier must be too many; too much goes only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: If I (A) were the principal, I (B) will allow students to use their phones (C) during breaks (D) as long as they behaved sensibly.
items.explanation: This is a second conditional (If I were ...), so the main clause takes would + verb, not will.

items.q: My father (A) usually listens to the radio (B) while he is driving, (C) but he cycles to the work (D) whenever the weather is fine.
options: but he cycles to the work
items.explanation: In the phrase go/cycle to work (meaning one's job) no article is used, like go to school or go to bed.

items.q: The recipe (A) says you should add (B) a pinch of salt to the dough, (C) but my brother uses (D) hardly no salt at all in his bread.
items.explanation: Hardly already has a negative meaning, so it cannot be combined with no; the correct form is hardly any.

items.q: Our science teacher (A) is believing that every student (B) can succeed (C) if they ask questions (D) whenever something is unclear.
items.explanation: Believe is a stative verb describing an opinion, so it is not normally used in the continuous form; use the present simple believes.

items.q: Every evening (A) my mother checks (B) whether we have made our homework (C) before she lets us (D) watch television.
options: whether we have made our homework
items.correction: whether we have done our homework
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with homework is do, not make: do your homework.

items.q: The girl (A) who won the piano competition (B) practises for hours every day, (C) that is why her fingers (D) move so quickly.
items.explanation: A relative clause that refers to the whole previous idea uses which after a comma; that cannot follow a comma in this way.

items.q: The information (A) on the school website (B) about the new timetable (C) is confusing, (D) and many parents has complained.
items.explanation: Many parents is a plural subject, so the auxiliary must be plural: have complained.

items.q: (A) Rarely we see snow in Da Lat, (B) so when it fell last week, (C) hundreds of tourists rushed (D) to take pictures.
options: Rarely we see snow in Da Lat
so when it fell last week
items.correction: Rarely do we see snow in Da Lat
items.explanation: When a negative adverb such as rarely or never starts the sentence, the subject and auxiliary are inverted: Rarely do we see.

items.q: My aunt (A) has worked (B) as nurse at the hospital near the airport (C) for almost twenty years, (D) often staying on duty all night.
items.explanation: A singular countable job title needs an article: as a nurse, as a teacher.

items.q: Both my brother (A) and I enjoy hiking in the mountains, (B) but neither my father (C) or my mother (D) has ever climbed Fansipan.
items.explanation: Neither must be paired with nor, never with or; either ... or and neither ... nor are fixed pairs.

items.q: Doctors (A) recommend that teenagers (B) sleep at least eight hours (C) a night (D) to stay health and alert.
items.explanation: After the linking verb stay an adjective is needed: healthy; health is a noun.

items.q: (A) Me and my friends are planning (B) to spend the summer (C) volunteering at an animal shelter (D) on the outskirts of the city.
options: Me and my friends are planning
on the outskirts of the city
items.correction: My friends and I are planning
items.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, so it must be the subject form I, and it is placed after the other people: My friends and I.

items.q: The train (A) to Nha Trang (B) leaves in nine o'clock sharp, (C) so we should be (D) at the station by half past eight.
options: at the station by half past eight
items.explanation: Clock times take the preposition at: at nine o'clock; in is used for months, years and parts of the day.

items.q: Linh (A) told me last week (B) that she (C) will visit her grandparents the following weekend, (D) but she changed her mind.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb (told), will shifts back to would in reported speech.

items.q: The company (A) has announced that (B) its new electric bus (C) will be tested on city routes (D) as soon as the batteries will arrive.
options: will be tested on city routes
as soon as the batteries will arrive
items.correction: as soon as the batteries arrive
items.explanation: In a future time clause after as soon as, when or until, the present simple is used, not will.

items.q: (A) This laptop is more cheaper than the one I saw online, (B) but its battery (C) lasts only (D) three hours.
options: This laptop is more cheaper than
items.explanation: A short adjective forms its comparative with -er (cheaper); adding more as well is a double comparative.

items.q: Our teacher gave us (A) plenty of time (B) to answer every questions, (C) but most of us (D) still finished at the last minute.
options: still finished at the last minute
items.explanation: Every is followed by a singular countable noun: every question; use all the questions for the plural.

items.q: It (A) took my grandfather nearly a year (B) to recover from his operation, (C) but he never gave in hope (D) of walking again.
options: took my grandfather nearly a year
but he never gave in hope
items.correction: but he never gave up hope
items.explanation: The phrasal verb that collocates with hope is give up (stop having); give in means to surrender and takes no object here.

items.q: The volunteers (A) collected (B) more than two hundred bags of rubbish (C) from the riverbank, (D) and they wanted to know where had it all come from.
options: more than two hundred bags of rubbish
and they wanted to know where had it all come from
items.correction: and they wanted to know where it had all come from
items.explanation: After wanted to know where the clause is an indirect question, so the subject comes before the auxiliary: where it had come from.
